To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the peak frequency of motor gamma oscillations is elevated when participants are required to select a response from multiple alternatives, while beta oscillations are more bilateral in response to distracting visual cues.

the peak frequency and the lateralization of movement‐related gamma oscillations are influenced by response competition, while the peak frequency and lateralization of the movement‐related beta event‐related oscillations are not.
The peak frequency of gamma oscillations is sensitive to response competition, while the beta ERD is sensitive to response selection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of distractors on the motor system.
how visual distractors modulate motor‐cortical function, and how the brain responds to response conflict.
the role of motor-related gamma activity in the brain, specifically in relation to the planning and execution of movement in the context of response competition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the peak frequency is modulated in the presence of response competition.
the peak frequency and amplitude of the gamma response is modulated by task parameters.
the peak frequency and amplitude of gamma activity is modulated by distractor‐induced response competition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
response conflict modulates motor‐related oscillations.
the beta and gamma oscillatory responses are modulated by the presence of distractor cues, and the peak frequency of MRGS is modulated by the level of response conflict.
the peak frequency in the MRGS response varies from trial to trail in individual participants and is modulated by the task parameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the peak frequency, but not the amplitude, of the MRGS was modulated by distractors, suggesting that the peak frequency is more sensitive to task demands.
the peak frequency in the gamma band is modulated by distractor cues that cause response competition.
the peak frequency, and not the amplitude, of the MRGS is modulated by the response conflict caused by distractors.
